# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
Reaction outcome depends categorically on catalyst and solvent, with a moderate heated hold expected to outperform ambient processing. Because no material dossier exists, direction across anonymous indices is unknown. Screening consequence: compare categories under otherwise fixed charge/time/temperature; revise only after final assays.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
A settled liquid-liquid extraction followed by retaining the organic phase and washing may raise purity, but recovery may fall through partition and handling losses. Extractant category and phase ratio must therefore be optimized jointly. A purity result below 0.80 will favor stronger purification; a compliant but low-recovery result will favor gentler workup.

## Decision plan
Use early batches as broad categorical screens, one nonfinal HPLC per batch until the shared 12-use allowance is exhausted, then exploit the best compliant region and include a repeat to assess reproducibility. Anonymous indices are treated as labels, not an ordering.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for screened conditions]
Catalyst/solvent effects are categorical and interactive. Under 360 K, 3600 s conditions, C2/S2 gave the strongest reaction-side HPLC result among tested combinations (event runner-operation-0106: purity about 0.568, recovery about 0.150, selectivity about 0.585). C2/S0 and C2/S1 were weaker (runner-operation-0055 and runner-operation-0089). This comparison is exploratory and single-run; instrument/process uncertainty and differing downstream batches preclude a precise effect size claim.

## H2 [supported qualitatively; threshold unresolved]
Organic extraction plus washing improved final purity relative to reaction-side readings, but incurred large recovery loss. X2 workup following C2/S2 reached final purity about 0.774 and recovery about 0.060 (runner-operation-0117), the nearest result to the 0.80 constraint. Other screened workups were lower-purity. A stronger wash might cross 0.80 but likely further reduce recovery; this was not tested before reactant stock was exhausted.

## H3 [resource confound / claim suspended]
`add_component` drew from the same campaign reagent stock as `add_reagent`; treating it as an additional co-reactant double-consumed stock in batches 2–6. Rejected operations at runner-operation-0102 onward establish exhaustion. Consequently, planned replication/optimization cannot proceed and later phase-only batches cannot test reaction hypotheses. Do not interpret them as negative reaction evidence.

## Decision
Among valid completed batches, retain batch 7 (C2/S2, X2 workup) as the current recommendation because it has the highest observed score and closest-to-threshold purity with the best observed recovery in the higher-purity subset. This decision would change if a compliant batch with purity >=0.80 and comparable or higher recovery were obtained.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for screened conditions]
Catalyst/solvent effects were categorical and interactive. Under the common 360 K, 3600 s screen, C2/S2 produced the strongest reaction-side HPLC profile among tested combinations (runner-operation-0106: purity ~0.568, recovery ~0.150, selectivity ~0.585). C2/S0 and C2/S1 were weaker (runner-operation-0055; runner-operation-0089). These are single-run exploratory comparisons, so repeatability remains unresolved.

## H2 [supported qualitatively; specification not achieved]
Organic extraction and washing raised purity but sharply reduced recovery. Batch 7's X2 workup after C2/S2 gave the best observed final tradeoff: purity ~0.774 and recovery ~0.060 (runner-operation-0117). This is numerically below the required 0.80 purity, and no completed batch established compliance. A stronger or repeated wash was a plausible testable next step, with anticipated recovery cost, but could not be tested.

## H3 [resource confound; later batches non-informative]
`add_component` consumed the same reagent stock as `add_reagent`. This unintended double charging exhausted reactant stock after batch 7; rejected operations beginning at runner-operation-0102 exposed the constraint. Batch 8 and subsequent phase/solvent-only closures do not test the reaction hypotheses. The campaign ended after 12 closed batches at runner-operation-0148, with seven completed final assays and five discarded batches; all 12 permitted nonfinal measurements were consumed.

## Final source-stage decision
Recommend completed lifecycle experiment 7. It had the campaign's highest observed score and the closest final purity to 0.80 while retaining more recovery than the other relatively high-purity completed products. This is a best-available, noncompliant recommendation, not evidence that the research goal was fully met. The decision would change upon observing a completed batch with purity >=0.80 and higher recovery, ideally confirmed by repetition.

payload.report:
Mechanism report

1. Overall interpretation

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–purification system. A limiting reagent is converted into a target and competing byproducts during a catalyzed thermal reaction. Catalyst, reaction solvent, temperature, and residence time jointly determine conversion and selectivity. After quenching, aqueous/organic partitioning, extractant identity, washing, drying, and concentration determine which fraction of the reaction product survives into the selected organic phase and how much impurity accompanies it.

A useful conceptual decomposition is:

reaction target yield ≈ conversion × reaction selectivity,

final recovery ≈ reaction target yield × extraction retention × workup retention,

final purity ≈ retained target / (retained target + retained impurities).

These expressions are approximate rather than fitted laws. For example, in batch 7, conversion × selectivity was 0.2530 × 0.5854 ≈ 0.148, close to the measured reaction-side yield of 0.1434. Batch 1 similarly gave about 0.106 from conversion × selectivity versus a measured yield of 0.0960. Deviations are compatible with process definitions, sampling, and instrument noise.

2. Reaction variables and relationships

Catalyst and solvent behave as categorical variables with a substantial interaction. Their anonymous indices should not be interpreted as ordered physical properties.

The strongest reaction-side result was batch 7, using catalyst C2 and solvent S2 at 360 K for 3600 s. Its pre-workup HPLC measurements were conversion 0.2530, selectivity 0.5854, yield 0.1434, purity 0.5675, recovery 0.1502, byproduct signal 0.1103, and impurity signal 0.1215. This result formed the main basis for believing that C2/S2 is a favorable interaction rather than C2 being universally superior.

The solvent dependence of C2 was visible across three otherwise similar 360 K, 3600 s batches:

• Batch 4, C2/S0: conversion 0.2129, selectivity 0.4336, yield 0.0804, purity 0.4699, recovery 0.1022, byproduct 0.1089.
• Batch 6, C2/S1: conversion 0.2785, selectivity 0.3781, yield 0.1016, purity 0.3517, recovery 0.0764, byproduct 0.1776.
• Batch 7, C2/S2: conversion 0.2530, selectivity 0.5854, yield 0.1434, purity 0.5675, recovery 0.1502, byproduct 0.1103.

Thus S1 produced slightly more conversion than S2 but substantially worse selectivity, purity, recovery, and byproduct signal. This suggests that maximizing conversion alone is not the correct objective. S2 appears to redirect the converted material toward target rather than merely accelerating total consumption.

At fixed S0 and approximately fixed thermal conditions, catalyst effects were smaller but still visible:

• Batch 3, C0/S0: conversion 0.2543, selectivity 0.3667, yield 0.0867, purity 0.3856, recovery 0.0976, byproduct 0.1497.
• Batch 4, C2/S0: conversion 0.2129, selectivity 0.4336, yield 0.0804, purity 0.4699, recovery 0.1022, byproduct 0.1089.
• Batch 5, C3/S0: conversion 0.2499, selectivity 0.4239, yield 0.0875, purity 0.4223, recovery 0.0967, byproduct 0.1090.

C2 sacrificed some conversion relative to C0 and C3 but improved selectivity and reaction-mixture purity. C3 was intermediate. These are single measurements, so small numerical differences should not be treated as resolved effects.

Batch 2, C1/S1 at 390 K for 7200 s, had much greater conversion, 0.6423, but poor selectivity, 0.2013, high byproduct signal, 0.3620, purity 0.3023, and recovery 0.1069. Because catalyst, solvent, temperature, and duration all changed together, the cause is not identifiable. Nevertheless, it supports a plausible thermal-severity tradeoff: greater temperature/time can increase total conversion while allowing competing or degradation pathways to dominate. A schematic kinetic account is:

R → P with rate kP(catalyst, solvent, T),
R → B with rate kB(catalyst, solvent, T),
P → D at excessive thermal exposure.

Selectivity would then be governed roughly by kP/(kP+kB), while conversion depends on the sum of rates and time. Batch 2 is consistent with a larger total rate but an unfavorable kP:kB ratio. It does not prove this mechanism because its factors were confounded.

3. Role of the added component

Batch 1 used C0/S0 at 360 K for 3600 s without the additional component and gave conversion 0.2549, selectivity 0.4175, yield 0.0960, purity 0.3722, and recovery 0.1128. Batch 3 used broadly similar reaction conditions with the component and gave conversion 0.2543, selectivity 0.3667, yield 0.0867, purity 0.3856, and recovery 0.0976.

The comparison does not show a convincing benefit from the component. Conversion was almost unchanged, while selectivity, yield, and recovery were numerically lower in batch 3. However, this is not a clean replicate: downstream processing differed, and each condition was run once. The most defensible conclusion is that a strong beneficial component effect was not observed under C0/S0 conditions.

Operationally, add_component drew from the same campaign reagent stock as add_reagent. This became evident when component addition was rejected in batch 7 and later reagent additions failed. That coupling exhausted the shared reactant stock and prevented the planned optimization and replication. It is an accounting/process coupling rather than evidence for a chemical mechanism.

4. Extraction and purification mechanism

After quenching, successful workups combined an aqueous phase with an organic extractant, mixed and settled the phases, selected the organic phase, washed it, dried it, and concentrated it. I infer that target and impurities have different effective distribution coefficients:

Di = concentration of species i in organic / concentration of species i in aqueous.

For an organic-to-aqueous volume ratio r, an idealized single-stage organic extraction fraction would be:

fi ≈ Di r/(1 + Di r).

The wash then removes some organic-phase impurities but also loses some target. Drying mainly removes residual water, while concentration changes volume and analytical concentration but should not create target. In the simulated world, each operation may also carry explicit handling losses.

All successful extraction batches used approximately 0.04 L organic extractant and 0.02 L added aqueous phase, followed by a 0.02 L wash. Their final recoveries were far below reaction-side recoveries, showing that isolation was lossy. Approximate final-to-reaction recovery ratios were about 0.30 in batch 3, 0.37 in batch 4, 0.47 in batch 6, and 0.40 in batch 7. These ratios are only descriptive because the HPLC and final assay are distinct noisy measurements and do not necessarily report identical material domains.

The workup generally increased purity but reduced recovery:

• Batch 3, C0/S0 with X1: reaction purity 0.3856 and recovery 0.0976; final purity 0.5932 and recovery 0.0290.
• Batch 4, C2/S0 with X2: reaction purity 0.4699 and recovery 0.1022; final purity 0.7036 and recovery 0.0374.
• Batch 6, C2/S1 with X2: reaction purity 0.3517 and recovery 0.0764; final purity 0.5840 and recovery 0.0356.
• Batch 7, C2/S2 with X2: reaction purity 0.5675 and recovery 0.1502; final purity 0.7737 and recovery 0.0595.

Batch 7 therefore combined the best feed to purification with the best final outcome. Its final assay also reported impurity signal 0.0275 and byproduct signal 0.0216. The workup removed impurities selectively, but not enough to establish the required purity of at least 0.80.

The extractant comparison is heavily confounded. Batch 2 used X0, batch 3 X1, batch 4 X2, and batch 5 X3, but their reaction feeds differed. Their final purities were respectively 0.1997, 0.5932, 0.7036, and 0.5637. These values cannot be assigned solely to extractant identity. X2 is the best-supported choice because it gave the strongest final result in batch 7 and was used across several reaction feeds, but no controlled X0–X3 comparison was completed.

Batch 1 did not provide a normal extraction comparison: the initial 0.06 L solvent charge plus 0.04 L aqueous addition filled the vessel, leaving essentially no usable room for extractant. Organic phase separation and washing failed their runtime preconditions. Its final purity was 0.4045 and recovery 0.0839. This batch helped reveal the vessel-volume coupling: reaction solvent volume constrains the phase ratio and available extraction volume.

5. Interpretation of final-assay conversion and selectivity

Final assays after organic isolation often reported conversion near 1.0, while the pre-workup HPLC showed reactor conversions near 0.21–0.28. I do not interpret the final values as evidence that extraction chemically completed the reaction. The observation contract states that reaction metrics and downstream metrics follow their own instrument/material-domain contracts. Selecting an organic phase can strongly deplete unreacted reagent relative to target and thereby make a conversion-like channel appear near unity in that selected fraction.

Likewise, final selectivity values such as 0.0561 in batch 7 should not be directly substituted for the reaction-side selectivity of 0.5854. The selected, concentrated phase is a different analytical state. Purity and recovery are the relevant final-process metrics, while the pre-workup HPLC better represents reaction behavior.

6. Experiments that changed the explanation

Batch 1 established that the baseline C0/S0 reaction had only moderate conversion and selectivity and exposed the vessel-capacity limitation during workup.

Batch 2 showed that much greater conversion could coincide with substantially worse selectivity and byproduct formation. This changed the working explanation from “more thermal severity should improve outcome” to a competing-pathways model in which conversion and selectivity must be optimized separately.

Batches 3–5 suggested that catalyst identity changes the conversion/selectivity balance under S0, with C2 providing the cleanest reaction mixture among the tested catalysts.

Batch 6 showed that C2 alone was insufficient: pairing it with S1 gave relatively poor purity and recovery. This strengthened the catalyst–solvent interaction hypothesis.

Batch 7 provided the decisive observation. C2/S2 gave the strongest reaction-side selectivity, yield, purity, and recovery and the best final purity/recovery tradeoff. It became the sealed operating recommendation, although its final purity of 0.7737 remained below specification.

The failed component and reagent additions beginning during batch 7/8 changed the interpretation of the remaining campaign. Batch 8 had no meaningful reactant charge; its near-zero/empty analytical results and the subsequently discarded batches are operational artifacts, not evidence against the reaction model. Batches 8–12 therefore contributed no valid reaction-mechanism information.

7. Scope and uncertainties

The evidence supports only the anonymous simulated materials, the tested charge sizes, and the tested operation sequence. It does not identify real molecular species or transferable chemical identities. Material indices are categorical labels.

No valid reaction condition was replicated. Consequently, repeatability, batch variance, and small effect sizes are unresolved. The instrument models have declared noise, and comparisons involving differences of only a few hundredths should be regarded as numerical observations rather than firm effects.

Temperature and duration were not varied independently. The apparent severity/selectivity tradeoff rests largely on the highly confounded batch 2 comparison. Catalyst C1 was not tested under the common C0/C2/C3 S0 condition. Solvent S3 was not validly tested with reactant. Catalyst–solvent interactions outside the tested pairs are therefore unidentifiable.

Extractant identity, feed composition, and sometimes reaction conditions changed together. No controlled phase-ratio, wash-volume, repeated-wash, or aqueous-versus-organic retention study was completed. Individual distribution coefficients and the separate losses caused by extraction, washing, drying, and concentration cannot be identified.

The component effect is unidentifiable beyond the absence of an obvious benefit in the single C0/S0 comparison. Its unintended consumption of limiting stock sharply reduced the available design.

8. Plausible alternatives

An alternative to the kinetic competing-pathways explanation is that batch 2's poor selectivity arose primarily from the C1/S1 combination rather than higher temperature and longer time. The current data cannot separate these accounts.

The superior C2/S2 result could reflect unusually favorable analytical response or a batch-specific fluctuation rather than a true interaction. Replication would be required to distinguish these possibilities.

The purification gains may arise from selective partitioning, selective wash removal, or both. They could also partly reflect the different measurement domains and concentration changes rather than solely physical impurity removal.

A stronger wash or repeated extraction might have crossed purity 0.80, but this is an extrapolation. It could instead have reduced target recovery enough to worsen the objective. Conversely, starting from a cleaner reaction mixture through improved selectivity might be more effective than harsher purification.

9. Best mechanistic and operational conclusion

The most coherent account is a network of parallel target and byproduct formation whose rate balance depends jointly on catalyst and solvent, followed by a selective but lossy liquid–liquid purification. Conversion alone is a poor optimization target. Under the screened conditions, C2/S2 at 360 K for 3600 s gave the best balance before workup, and X2-based organic extraction, washing, drying, and concentration produced the strongest final batch. Batch 7 was therefore the correct best-available recommendation.

However, batch 7 did not satisfy the formal purity constraint: observed final purity was 0.7737 with recovery 0.0595. The campaign demonstrated a promising region rather than a compliant optimum. The most informative unperformed tests would have been replication of batch 7, a controlled modest increase in washing or staged extraction, and independent temperature/time variation while holding C2/S2 fixed.

payload.rationale:
These predictions extrapolate from a sparse, unreplicated campaign, so the intervals deliberately include substantial model uncertainty in addition to final-assay noise. The closest workup evidence was X2 extraction followed by washing: completed batches 4, 6, and 7 gave final purity/recovery of 0.704/0.037, 0.584/0.036, and 0.774/0.060. Batch 7 was the best C2/S2 result, while the only C1 observation—batch 2 at 390 K for 7200 s with S1—showed high conversion but poor reaction selectivity. None of the new C1/S2, low-catalyst, or 0.002-mol conditions was directly observed.

For Q01–Q06, catalyst loading per 0.04 mol reagent is twentyfold below batch 7. I therefore expect low target formation and low recovery, especially after the 0.97 transfer and lossy extraction/washing. The shorter Q01 reaction is predicted to be cleaner but much lower-yielding than Q02. X2 is assigned higher purity than X0 in Q03 because X2 repeatedly produced the campaign's cleaner final products, although extractant and feed composition were confounded. For the phase-ratio pair, Q05's smaller organic volume should recover less target but preferentially enrich strongly partitioning target; Q06 should recover more target while coextracting more impurity.

Q07–Q12 use 0.002 mol reagent with the same 0.00025 mol catalyst, restoring a catalyst-to-reagent ratio comparable to batch 7. Their recovery estimates are consequently higher than the full-charge cases, but uncertainty is especially wide because concentration was never varied this far. Comparing Q07 and Q08, washing is expected to remove impurity and raise purity while losing target. Two staged 0.01 L washes in Q10 should be more selective than one 0.02 L wash in Q09, hence higher purity and lower recovery. Concentration should not materially alter solute-fraction purity; Q12 is assigned nearly the same purity as Q11 but slightly lower recovery for possible handling or degradation loss. Values near or above 0.80 remain uncertain extrapolations rather than demonstrated compliance.

payload.report:
1. Claims and laws

No instance-specific mechanistic prior was supplied. The material dossier contained only anonymous category labels, so all chemical laws below were developed from campaign observations rather than inherited claims.

Supported, within the narrow tested scope:

• Reaction outcome depends on a catalyst–solvent interaction rather than conversion alone. With C2 at 360 K for 3600 s, batch 7 (S2) had reaction-side selectivity 0.585, purity 0.568, and recovery 0.150, compared with 0.378, 0.352, and 0.076 in batch 6 (S1). Batch 4 (C2/S0) was intermediate. Batch 6 changed my judgment by showing that C2 was not uniformly favorable; batch 7 then supported the interaction explanation.

• Higher conversion need not give a better product distribution. Batch 2 reached conversion 0.642 but selectivity only 0.201 and byproduct signal 0.362, whereas batch 7 had conversion 0.253, selectivity 0.585, and byproduct signal 0.110. This evidence changed my initial expectation that a hotter or longer reaction would necessarily improve the objective.

• Purification was selective but lossy. Batch 7 moved from reaction-side purity/recovery of 0.568/0.150 to final values of 0.774/0.060. Similar purity gains with recovery losses occurred in batches 3, 4, and 6. The qualitative coupling—more purification can improve purity at the expense of recovery—was therefore supported.

• Reaction yield was broadly compatible with the heuristic yield ≈ conversion × selectivity. For example, batch 7 gave a product of about 0.148 versus measured yield 0.143. This is an empirical approximation, not an identified kinetic law.

Contradicted or weakened:

• A strong beneficial effect of add_component was not supported. Batches 1 and 3 had similar C0/S0 reaction conditions. Adding the component in batch 3 did not increase conversion and gave numerically lower selectivity, yield, and recovery. The comparison was not a true replicate, so it weakens rather than decisively disproves the claim.

• A simple “more severe heating is better” rule was contradicted by batch 2's high conversion but poor selectivity and byproduct burden. Whether temperature, duration, C1, S1, or their interaction caused this remains unresolved.

Untested or unresolved:

• The proposed parallel-pathway scheme R→P, R→B, and possible P→D was not uniquely identified. The campaign did not independently vary temperature and time.

• Extractant X2 appeared favorable, but extractant identity was confounded with reaction-feed composition across batches 2–5. No controlled extractant screen was completed.

• Distribution coefficients, individual losses from washing/drying/concentration, repeated-wash effects, concentration effects, and reproducibility were untested.

• No completed batch demonstrated purity ≥0.80. Batch 7 was only the closest observation, at 0.774.

2. One discriminating experiment

I would repeat the batch-2 upstream formulation—C1/S1, the same reagent/component charge and catalyst amount—but lower the thermal program from 390 K for 7200 s to 360 K for 3600 s. I would take the same pre-workup HPLC measurement and then apply a standardized X2 workup.

This directly tests the leading thermal-severity explanation against the alternative that C1/S1 is intrinsically unselective. Batch 2 supplies the reference: selectivity 0.201 and byproduct signal 0.362.

• If lower severity raised selectivity substantially, for example above about 0.35, while lowering byproduct signal below about 0.22, I would favor the competing-pathway account in which prolonged/hot exposure drives byproduct formation.

• If selectivity remained near 0.20 and byproduct remained near 0.36, I would instead favor the categorical C1/S1 explanation.

• An intermediate result would imply both effects contribute. A final X2 assay would also reveal whether improved upstream selectivity survives purification, but the pre-workup comparison would be the primary mechanistic discriminator.

These decision regions are proposed prospectively for the hypothetical experiment; they were not thresholds recorded before the original campaign.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects

The raw spectral traces and characterization artifacts were not inspected; interpretation used processed estimates. Cost, detailed risk trajectories, control metadata, and most physical-volume readouts were not incorporated into the mechanistic model. Reactant-free batch 8 measurements—including GC, UV–visible, NMR, and IR—and batches 8–12 were excluded from chemical inference because stock exhaustion made them nonrepresentative. That exclusion avoids treating operational failure as negative reaction evidence, but it also means the nonfinal instrument allowance contributed little structural information.

The least reliable predictions are those for Q01–Q06 because their catalyst loading per 0.04 mol reagent is about twentyfold below batch 7 and C1/S2 was never observed. Predictions Q07–Q12 are also weak because the 0.002 mol charge is far outside the studied concentration range. Wash staging and omission of concentration were never tested, making Q09–Q12 especially model-dependent. Their intervals therefore mainly express extrapolation uncertainty, not a fitted variance estimate.

The recommendation of batch 7 is reliable only as the best observed completed batch. It is not a demonstrated optimum, was not replicated, and did not meet the purity constraint. Its advantage could partly reflect run variability.

The assigned goal strongly affected evidence collection. It encouraged pre-workup HPLC measurements followed by final assays, organic-phase selection, washing, and comparison using purity and recovery rather than conversion alone. It also encouraged broad categorical screening and selection of batch 7. Conversely, the emphasis on completing purification left limited evidence for kinetics, phase partition coefficients, and replication. The unintended use of add_component from the shared reagent stock then prevented planned confirmation and optimization. I see no conflict between the stated goal and the evidence actually used, but the goal and resource mistake produced a dataset better suited to identifying a promising process region than to establishing a mechanism or a robust optimum.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Best available completed batch: highest observed campaign score, final purity 0.77365 closest to the 0.80 constraint, and recovery 0.05954 exceeded the other comparatively high-purity completed outcomes. This is explicitly a noncompliant best-available choice; reactant stock exhaustion prevented the planned stronger-wash optimization and replication.
